_comment: Deliberate keep-raw decisions, per plan section 7.5. These are the sites
where forcing the ORM would hurt readability and a rewrite bug would be
silent and expensive. Every rule must carry a reason: the plan forbids
silent deferral, so a site can only leave the raw count by being converted
or by appearing here with a justification that survived review.
Rules match on file plus optional function. The extractor applies them on
every regeneration, so these decisions are declarative rather than a
Each keep-raw site becomes an input to migration Phase 4 (the dialect
port), and per 7.5 should sit behind a thin repository layer with its own

rules.reason: Migration harness. These sites execute the original raw SQL by design, in order to compare it against the replacement ORM call, so they are not migration targets.
rules.porting: Not applicable: this is the migration harness itself, not production code. Its raw SQL exists to compare against production SQL and is deliberately unconverted.

rules.reason: Builds a SQLite export file, not a query against the Percona cluster. Out of scope for the MySQL-to-ORM work and unaffected by the engine migration.
rules.porting: Not applicable: this writes SQLite, for the user data export. It is unaffected by the MySQL-to-PostgreSQL migration and should not be counted in the Phase 4 estimate.

rules.reason: Threads a raw *sql.DB rather than a *gorm.DB. buildDump unwraps database.DBConn.DB() and passes that handle through buildPlan/scanIDs/runDBSpec/gatherEmails, so these statements run on the SAME Percona connection as the rest of the API. NOT SQLite, and NOT runtime-varying in the way the previous category claimed: an earlier version of this reason asserted kinship with userdump/sqlite.go, which was wrong - sqlite.go writes the export FILE and is genuinely out of scope, whereas these read the production database and are ordinary conversion candidates. The blocker is the handle type, and it is narrower than the redesign an earlier reason described: each of these functions only ever needed something it can query MySQL through, which *gorm.DB already is, so it is a uniform parameter-type swap across the collectors and their two callers rather than a structural split. scanIDs is the exception that genuinely stays: it is a generic run-this-text-and-scan-the-first-column helper shared by three different fixed statements, so its SQL belongs to its call sites, the same precedent as database/insert.go ExecInsertGetID and the database/retry.go wrappers.
rules.porting: PostgreSQL: no dialect obstacle - these are ordinary SELECTs. The one thing to revisit on port is information_schema.tables, whose table_schema = DATABASE() idiom is MySQL-shaped; PostgreSQL spells the equivalent with current_schema() or the pg_catalog views.

rules.reason: Layer 3 harness infrastructure. Reads the shadow batch flag from the config table by design and is not a migration target, in the same way the ormharness package is not.
rules.porting: Not applicable: migration harness, as above.

rules.reason: The SELECT ... FOR UPDATE runs through tx.QueryRow on a raw *sql.Tx taken from db.DB().Begin(), and shares that transaction with a following raw UPDATE (existing-chat path) or INSERT (new-chat path) that needs sql.Result.LastInsertId() on the SAME connection to report the row the lock protected. Converting any of these three in isolation would either take it outside the transaction, defeating the row lock the unique key can't provide (user2 is NULL, and MySQL treats NULLs as distinct in unique indexes), or force the whole function onto db.Transaction() - a per-site redesign, not a mechanical conversion. NOTE: this function's other two raw statements - the two 'INSERT IGNORE INTO chat_roster' calls after the transaction commits/rolls back - are NOT part of this lock and have been converted separately (sites 1c2cfaaab39b, 57f83af68a60); this reason covers only the three still inside the shared tx. SECURITY (reviewed): this statement interpolates values into SQL TEXT rather than binding them, so it was checked for injection. Every interpolated value is numeric and formatted through strconv or a %d/%f verb - group ids as uint64 via FormatUint, bounding-box coordinates as float32 via FormatFloat, keepChat/onlyChat as uint64 parsed with ParseUint - and no numeric type can carry a SQL metacharacter. That makes it safe TODAY, but the safety comes entirely from the parameter TYPES and nothing enforces it: changing any of these parameters to a string, or adding a string-typed fragment alongside them, opens an injection with no test that would fail. Treat the numeric types as load-bearing when editing this code.
rules.porting: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... RETURNING id. This is the one category that gets EASIER on Postgres - RETURNING is part of the statement, so the id comes back with the insert and the connection-scoped LAST_INSERT_ID() problem disappears entirely. GORM exposes it via clause.Returning, so these sites may become convertible during the port rather than staying raw.
rules.category: INSERT whose generated id is read back

rules.reason: The ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE clause here is 'arrangedat = NOW()' with no 'id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id)' forcing, so on a duplicate-key hit MySQL's LAST_INSERT_ID() doesn't report the existing row's id - the current raw code already returns 0 in that case. This is a pre-existing APPLICATION-LEVEL bug, not a GORM limitation (GORM reads LastInsertId from the sql.Result of the SAME statement Create() issues, which is not connection-scoped - the earlier 'GORM doesn't surface LastInsertId for an ODKU' framing recorded here was wrong about the mechanism, per the adversarial review's finding that this reason class has been wrong before). A mechanical port would faithfully reproduce the 0-on-duplicate bug; fixing it (adding id-forcing to the UPDATE clause) is a deliberate behaviour change tracked separately, not a wave conversion. This function's other raw statement (the chat-exists COUNT, site f06281f794b9) has been converted separately - it is an ordinary literal-WHERE query unrelated to this ODKU insert.

rules.reason: Infrastructure wrapper: takes an already-built statement from a caller and retries it. The SQL belongs to the calling site, which is inventoried separately.
rules.porting: PostgreSQL: the retry predicates match MySQL error numbers (1213 deadlock, 1205 lock wait timeout, 2006/2013 connection loss). Postgres uses SQLSTATE instead - 40P01 deadlock_detected, 55P03 lock_not_available, class 08 for connection failures. This is infrastructure rather than a query, but it must be ported or retries silently stop working, which shows up as user-facing errors under load rather than as a test failure.

rules.reason: DDL, not DML: this function runs DROP TEMPORARY TABLE IF EXISTS pc followed by CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE pc AS (SELECT locationid FROM authorities INNER JOIN locations_spatial ON authorities.id = ? AND ST_Contains(...)) inside a dbresolver.Write-pinned transaction (temp tables are connection-local, so the pin matters as much as the DDL). GORM's clause vocabulary has no CREATE/DROP TABLE clause type - this isn't a workaround gap, GORM's own Migrator falls back to db.Exec() with literal SQL for exactly this reason, which is what this code already does. The several ordinary SELECT/GROUP BY queries later in the same function that read the temp table back (e.g. site f3d569f16f75) are NOT part of this blocker and are already converted - only the two DDL statements themselves stay raw. Previously mislabelled under the file-wide 'Spatial: ST_*/MBR* risk' reason: the ST_Contains call inside the CREATE...AS SELECT is incidental to a DDL mechanism gap that has nothing to do with geometry semantics. EVIDENCE (researched, not assumed): GORM has no mechanism here. clause.With is an empty struct in gorm.io/gorm/clause/with.go with no Build or Name method, so it does not even satisfy clause.Interface; Migrator.DropTable is itself implemented as a literal Exec; and CreateTable needs a registered struct schema, so it cannot express AS SELECT. SESSION AFFINITY, which is the real risk with a connection-scoped temporary table behind a read/write-split pool, was checked and is NOT a bug here: GetStatsByAuthority takes one pinned transaction and routes every statement - both DDL statements, every read from the temp table, and the final DROP - through a writer() closure over that transaction, never through database.DBConn. Confirmed empirically against two disposable MySQL instances that dbresolver skips routing entirely once ConnPool is a transaction (its callbacks guard on isTransaction), so a transaction pins everything to one connection. The current code is correct.
rules.porting: PostgreSQL/PostGIS: most ST_* names carry over, but three things change. ST_Distance_Sphere becomes ST_DistanceSphere or a cast to geography; MySQL's axis order for SRID 4326 is lat/lng while PostGIS is lng/lat, which silently transposes coordinates if unhandled; and MBRContains and friends have no PostGIS equivalent - use && (bounding-box overlap) or ST_Intersects. Getting the axis order wrong shows wrong nearby posts without erroring.

rules.reason: Not runtime-varying the way the extractor's placeholder implies: the two "LIMIT %d" verbs are utils.NEWSFEED_EVENTS_PER_FEED (20) and utils.NEWSFEED_ALERTS_PER_FEED (5), Go constants that never change - once resolved this call site is a single fixed 4-way UNION (regular posts / event-and-volunteering posts / alerts in the member's alert box / pinned alerts from anywhere), not a many-shapes site. It stays raw because GORM ships no UNION clause (same reason as chat/chatroom.go's listChats, site 537a2764efde) and a Table()/Where() chain cannot express four differently-shaped SELECTs combined by UNION, not because of any remaining toggle. gotAlertBox - the toggle the sibling site 7558e63cd067 has - does NOT apply here: this call site only runs when gotLatLng is true, which always implies gotAlertBox is also true (both derive from the same resolved userLat/userLng), so the alert arm here is unconditionally the MBRContains form. Previously described as multi-toggle runtime-varying alongside its sibling; that was inaccurate for this specific site. EVIDENCE (researched, not assumed): GORM v1.31.0 contains no UNION support at all - zero occurrences of the word anywhere in its source, and the query clause list is the fixed set SELECT/FROM/WHERE/GROUP BY/ORDER BY/LIMIT/FOR in callbacks/callbacks.go. Upstream issues go-gorm/gorm#5552 and #6759 both request it and both remain open. A third-party plugin (WinterYukky/gorm-extra-clause-plugin) does register a real UNION clause properly, but it does not rescue these sites: GORM's Statement has ONE ORDER BY slot and ONE LIMIT slot, so an arm carrying its own LIMIT has it silently discarded rather than rejected - confirmed by rendering. Every arm here carries its own LIMIT, so this is a structural property of the statement model, not a missing feature a plugin patches. Converting the UNION keyword alone would also not reduce the raw surface: it trades one raw statement for several raw arms plus raw glue.
rules.porting: PostgreSQL: UNION is standard and ports unchanged. Raw here because GORM ships no UNION clause, not because of dialect. The spatial functions (MBRContains, ST_SRID, ST_Contains) need the same PostGIS translations noted elsewhere for MySQL SRID 4326/3857 spatial sites: MBRContains has no PostGIS equivalent (use && bounding-box overlap or ST_Intersects), and MySQL's axis order for SRID 4326 is lat/lng while PostGIS is lng/lat, which silently transposes coordinates if unhandled.

Session-scoped alongside the CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE it pairs with in the same function; see GetStatsByAuthority's dbresolver.Write-pinned transaction comment for why the pairing matters. EVIDENCE (researched, not assumed): GORM has no mechanism here. clause.With is an empty struct in gorm.io/gorm/clause/with.go with no Build or Name method, so it does not even satisfy clause.Interface; Migrator.DropTable is itself implemented as a literal Exec; and CreateTable needs a registered struct schema, so it cannot express AS SELECT. SESSION AFFINITY, which is the real risk with a connection-scoped temporary table behind a read/write-split pool, was checked and is NOT a bug here: GetStatsByAuthority takes one pinned transaction and routes every statement - both DDL statements, every read from the temp table, and the final DROP - through a writer() closure over that transaction, never through database.DBConn. Confirmed empirically against two disposable MySQL instances that dbresolver skips routing entirely once ConnPool is a transaction (its callbacks guard on isTransaction), so a transaction pins everything to one connection. The current code is correct.
rules.porting: PostgreSQL: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE becomes CREATE TEMP TABLE (or keep TEMPORARY, both are accepted). The behavioural difference that matters: Postgres temp tables are per-SESSION and dropped at session end, and CREATE TABLE ... AS does not accept MySQL's index hints. The surrounding code already pins one connection for the temp table's lifetime, which is what makes this work on either engine.

No single golden can describe every form it can take, so Layer 1 parity - one rendered statement compared against one golden - is impossible by construction. rules.reason: listChats builds one enormous SELECT (chat_rooms.go:1148-1205) by string concatenation across ~60 lines, not a fixed template: it embeds a WITH-CTE ("WITH cm AS (... ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY chatid ORDER BY id DESC) AS rn ...) SELECT * FROM cm WHERE rn = 1") inside a derived-table LEFT JOIN to get each chat rooms most recent visible message, alongside 8 other LEFT JOINs (groups, two user rows, three image lookups, chat_messages, messages) and 11 positional bind args threaded through by hand (myid appears 6 times at different positions). The chatid/chat_rooms.id IN-list (idlist) is ALSO spliced as literal decimal text via strings.Join, twice, into this same statement - not a second independent site, the same one. GORM has no CTE or window-function builder, so this cannot become a chain; it could in principle be rewritten with db.Raw plus a bound []uint64 slice for idlist (mechanically identical to the literal-int fix applied elsewhere in this file - handleAllSeen 3519e352775b, getModeratorChatIDs d44b753b35c8), but the surrounding 11-bind, 9-join CTE is large enough that a hand conversion risks a silently wrong bind position or a dropped join condition in the live chat list, with no fixed golden to catch it - Layer 1 text parity is impossible by construction (no single form), and Layer 2 result parity would need a GORM chain to compare against, which does not exist here. Left raw deliberately, not for lack of trying: see plans/active/orm-keepraw-adversarial-review.md Tier 9. rules.porting: PostgreSQL: the WITH-CTE and ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) both carry over unchanged - this is standard SQL, not a MySQL extension. JSON_EXTRACT(col, '$.path') becomes col->>'path' (or col#>>'{path}' for nested paths). The real port risk is the same as everywhere else in this file: an implicit reliance on MySQL correlated-subquery evaluation order or its permissive JSON-in-boolean-context coercion (CASE WHEN JSON_EXTRACT(...) IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE JSON_EXTRACT(...) END used directly as a boolean) that Postgres will reject or evaluate differently and needs an explicit cast.

rules.reason: Variable-length OR-ed predicate list, NOT a UNION. The previous reason came from a shared template describing the wider category and did not fit these four: each is a single SELECT whose WHERE gains one predicate per input word (word LIKE ?, damlevlim(...), soundex = ...), so the arm-count reasoning that applies to a real UNION does not apply at all. Recorded accurately so nobody later reasons about it as a UNION case and reaches for a UNION mechanism that would not help. rules.reason: Proven, but still raw - NOT converted. The statement cannot be expressed as a GORM chain (ListMessagesMT assembles it at runtime: a UNION whose arm count follows the input, or a SET list built one fragment per optional field). The technique used instead was to extract a pure builder function and prove its output against an independently-written expectation with a parametrized-shape or fieldwise parity test, which is genuine verification and is why this site has a test naming it. What it is not is a conversion: the raw db.Raw/db.Exec call is still there, and the builder just moved the SQL text one function along. It was briefly recorded as converted, which double-counted the statement - once as converted under the id the text used to hash to, and again as raw under the id the extractor assigns now the text lives in the builder. EVIDENCE (researched, not assumed): GORM v1.31.0 contains no UNION support at all - zero occurrences of the word anywhere in its source, and the query clause list is the fixed set SELECT/FROM/WHERE/GROUP BY/ORDER BY/LIMIT/FOR in callbacks/callbacks.go.
